questions.q: A herder in a settlement on the Saraswati drops one pebble in a clay pot for every cow that leaves and takes one out for every cow that returns. This matching of one object to one object is called:
questions.a: one-to-one correspondence

questions.q: The symbol Z for the integers comes from a German word. Which word, and what does it mean?
questions.a: Zahlen, meaning numbers

questions.q: One column of the Ishango bone has notch groups of 11, 13, 17 and 19. How does the book describe these numbers?
questions.a: The prime numbers between 10 and 20
o: All the odd numbers between 10 and 20
A count of the days of a lunar month

questions.q: Using Brahmagupta's rule for the product of a debt and a fortune, (–7) × 6 equals:
Kiran owes ₹35 to Anil and ₹20 to Bhavna and has no money. Written as an integer, his total position is:
At 6 a.m. a hill town in Himachal records –3 °C. By afternoon the temperature rises by 11 °C and by midnight it falls by 14 °C. The midnight temperature is:

Read the statements.
Statement 1: Brahmagupta defined zero as the result of subtracting a number from itself, a – a = 0.
Statement 2: The natural numbers are always closed under subtraction.
Statement 3: The product of two debts is a fortune.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): (–5) + (–4) = –9.
Reason (R): A fortune plus a fortune is a fortune.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. The sum –9 comes from the rule 'a debt plus a debt is a debt' (owing ₹5 and borrowing ₹4 more makes a debt of ₹9); the fortune rule is a different rule.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A Lothal merchant receives 7 copper ingots for every 3 bags of cotton he brings. (a) How many ingots does he receive for 18 bags? (b) He leaves the market with 35 ingots. How many bags did he bring?
questions.a: (a) 18 bags is 6 groups of 3 bags, so 6 × 7 = 42 ingots. (b) 35 ingots is 5 groups of 7, so 5 × 3 = 15 bags.
s: Part (a): finds 6 groups of 3 bags and 42 ingots
Part (b): reverses the ratio to get 5 groups and 15 bags

questions.q: (a) Give one example to show that the natural numbers are not closed under subtraction. (b) Name the collection of numbers in which that subtraction first has an answer, and state the answer for your example.
questions.a: (a) 4 – 9 is not a natural number (for example 3 – 5 has no natural-number answer). (b) The integers; 4 – 9 = –5 (and 3 – 5 = –2).
s: Part (a): a subtraction of a larger natural number from a smaller one
Part (b): names the integers and gives the negative answer

questions.q: (a) Calculate (–9) × (–6) and (–9) × 6. (b) In the language of debts, explain why the first answer is positive.
questions.a: (a) (–9) × (–6) = 54 and (–9) × 6 = –54. (b) Multiplying by a negative number removes debts: taking away six debts of ₹9 each leaves a person ₹54 richer, so the product of two debts is a fortune.
s: Part (b): explains the product of two debts as removing debts, giving a fortune

questions.q: State Brahmagupta's rules for zero: what happens when zero is added to a number, subtracted from a number, and when a number is multiplied by zero?
questions.a: a + 0 = a, so the number is unchanged by adding zero; a – 0 = a, so it is unchanged by subtracting zero; a × 0 = 0, so any number times zero is zero.
s: States a + 0 = a and a – 0 = a

questions.q: Babylonians and Mayans used a symbol for an empty column, yet the book credits Brahmagupta with making zero a number. (a) What did the earlier symbol do? (b) What did Brahmagupta add that made zero a number?
questions.a: (a) It was only a placeholder marking an empty column in a number; it was not added, subtracted or multiplied. (b) He defined zero as a – a and gave rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with it.
s: Part (a): identifies the earlier symbol as a placeholder
Part (b): says Brahmagupta defined zero and gave arithmetic rules for it

questions.q: Meera says, 'Subtracting zero from a debt wipes the debt out, so –8 – 0 = 0.' Do you agree? Give the rule that decides it.
questions.a: No. Brahmagupta's rule says a debt minus zero is a debt: a – 0 = a. So –8 – 0 = –8, and the debt is unchanged.
s: Gives the verdict that Meera is wrong
Quotes the rule a – 0 = a (a debt minus zero is a debt)

questions.q: Show that the equation x + 7 = 3 has no solution among the natural numbers but has one among the integers.
questions.a: If x were a natural number, x + 7 would be at least 1 + 7 = 8, which is bigger than 3, so no natural x works. In the integers x = 3 – 7 = –4 and –4 + 7 = 3.
s: Shows x + 7 is at least 8 for natural x, so it cannot equal 3
Finds x = 3 – 7 = –4 as the integer solution

questions.q: Make up a short school tuck-shop story that is described by the integer expression (–250) + 400 + (–120). Say what the final answer means in your story.
questions.a: Sample: the tuck shop begins the week owing ₹250 to the supplier (–250), earns ₹400 on sports day (+400) and pays ₹120 for repairs (–120). The total is –250 + 400 – 120 = 30, a fortune of ₹30.
s: Story uses a debt of 250, a gain of 400 and a loss of 120
Interprets 30 as a fortune (money in hand) of ₹30

questions.q: A spice trader borrows ₹640 on Monday, makes a profit of ₹1,150 on Thursday and suffers a loss of ₹720 on Saturday. (a) Write the week as a sum of integers. (b) Find his standing at the end of the week. (c) He then takes on 3 more debts of ₹150 each. Write this as a product and find his new standing. (d) How much fortune must he earn to clear all his debts?
questions.a: (a) (–640) + 1150 + (–720). (b) –640 + 1150 – 720 = –210, a debt of ₹210. (c) (–150) × 3 = –450, so the standing is –210 – 450 = –660. (d) He needs a fortune of ₹660 to bring his standing back to zero.
s: Part (d): says ₹660 of fortune is needed to reach zero

questions.q: (a) Use fortunes and debts to explain why (–6) × (–5) = 30. (b) Use a debt story to explain why 8 – (–3) = 11. (c) Calculate (–36) ÷ 4.
questions.a: (a) A debt of ₹6 taken away 5 times (–6 repeated with a negative count) removes ₹30 of debt, so you are ₹30 richer: (–6) × (–5) = +30. (b) Having ₹8 and having a debt of ₹3 taken away leaves you ₹3 richer, so 8 – (–3) = 8 + 3 = 11. (c) (–36) ÷ 4 = –9.
s: Part (a): explains 30 as the removal of five debts of ₹6
Part (b): explains subtracting a debt as gaining, 8 + 3 = 11

questions.q: Dhana Mart in Jaipur records fortunes as positive and debts as negative. Monday: sales ₹4,200 and shop rent paid ₹1,500. Tuesday: stock bought on credit ₹3,800. Wednesday: sales ₹2,900 and wages paid ₹1,750. (a) Write Monday's net result as an integer sum and find it. (b) Find the shop's standing at the end of Wednesday. (c) From Thursday a generator is rented at ₹400 a day for 3 days; write this as a product of integers and give its value. (d) With the generator the shop earns a net ₹350 a day from sales on those 3 days. Find the standing at the end of Saturday, and say whether renting is wise if the owner does not want to end in debt.
questions.a: (a) 4200 + (–1500) = 2700. (b) 2700 + (–3800) + 2900 + (–1750) = 50, a fortune of ₹50. (c) (–400) × 3 = –1200. (d) Sales of 3 × 350 = 1050 and rent of –1200 give –150, so the standing is 50 – 150 = –100, a debt of ₹100. Renting leaves the shop in debt, so it is not wise if debt must be avoided (closing keeps the ₹50 fortune); renting is only worth it if the owner accepts a small debt for keeping customers.
s: Part (d): standing –100 and a justified decision

questions.q: A herder in a settlement beside the Saraswati keeps a pebble pot to check his cattle: one pebble goes in for each cow that leaves in the morning and one comes out for each cow that returns. This morning 56 cows left and 53 returned by evening. (a) Name the idea behind the pebble method and say how many pebbles remain. (b) Later two missing cows are found at a neighbour's field and return. How many pebbles remain, and which number would mean 'all cows are back', and why is it missing from {1, 2, 3, …}? (c) The neighbour asks ₹30 a day as grazing charge for each of those 2 cows for 3 days. Write the charge as a product of a debt and a count, and find it. (d) The herder has ₹150 in hand. Does he stay in fortune after paying? Justify.
questions.a: (a) One-to-one correspondence; 56 – 53 = 3 pebbles remain. (b) 3 – 2 = 1 pebble remains; the number would be 0 when all return, but zero is not in the natural numbers {1, 2, 3, …}; it became a number only with Brahmagupta (the integers include it). (c) 2 cows × 3 days = 6 cow-days, so the charge is (–30) × 6 = –180, a debt of ₹180. (d) 150 – 180 = –30, so he ends with a debt of ₹30 and does not stay in fortune; he is ₹30 short.
s: Part (b): 1 pebble; zero is absent from the natural numbers
Part (d): 150 – 180 = –30, a debt, so he is short by ₹30

questions.q: Which description matches the book's definition of a rational number?
questions.a: A number that can be written as p/q with p and q integers and q ≠ 0
o: A number that can be written as p/q with p and q integers and q ≠ 0
A number that can be written as p/q with p and q natural numbers
A number that can be written as p/q with p ≠ 0 and q any integer
A number that is a fraction with a positive numerator and denominator

questions.q: Which of these is NOT equivalent to –1/3?
Rational numbers are closed under division provided that:
questions.a: the divisor is not zero

questions.q: Which pair of rational numbers is equal by the test ad = bc?
The product (3/4) × (–8/9) equals:
A sweet-maker in Mathura has 18 3/4 kg of besan, and one batch of laddoos needs 1 7/8 kg. How many batches can he make?
Aman adds 2/5 and 3/10 by adding the numerators and adding the denominators, getting 5/15. Which statement is right?
questions.a: The sum is 7/10; both fractions must first be written with a common denominator
o: The sum is 7/10; the denominators must be made equal first
The sum is 5/15, because the rule adds tops and bottoms
The sum is 1/2, because only the numerators are added
The sum is 3/25, because the two fractions are multiplied

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: Two rational numbers a/b and c/d are equal if a + d = b + c.
Statement 2: For rational numbers p, q and r, p(q + r) = pq + pr.
Statement 3: The quotient of two rational numbers is always a rational number.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 5/0 is a rational number.
Reason (R): In p/q the denominator q must not be zero.
questions.a: The assertion is false but the reason is true: rational numbers need q ≠ 0, so 5/0 is not a rational number.
o: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.

questions.q: (a) Prove, using ad = bc, that 6/15 and 10/25 are equal. (b) Write –18/42 in its lowest form and state the common factor you divided by.
questions.a: (a) 6 × 25 = 150 and 15 × 10 = 150, so ad = bc and the numbers are equal. (b) Dividing top and bottom by 6 gives –18/42 = –3/7.

questions.q: (a) Find 5/12 + 7/8. (b) Hence find 7/8 – 5/12.
Explain why the definition of a rational number needs q ≠ 0.
questions.a: p/0 would have to be a number n with n × 0 = p. But every number times 0 is 0, so for p ≠ 0 no such number exists; division by zero has no meaning, so q is not allowed to be 0.
s: Links p/q to a number n with n × q = p
Shows that n × 0 = 0 can never equal a non-zero p

questions.q: (a) Write 8 and –13 in the form p/q. (b) What does this show about integers and rational numbers?
questions.a: (a) 8 = 8/1 and –13 = –13/1. (b) Every integer can be written as p/q with q = 1, so the integers (and the natural and whole numbers) are included among the rational numbers.
s: Part (b): concludes integers are rational numbers

questions.q: (a) Write the additive inverses of 19/7 and –5/8. (b) Show where the minus sign may stand when you write –19/7, using the forms the book gives.
questions.a: (a) –19/7 and 5/8. (b) The sign may sit with the numerator or the denominator: –19/7 = (–19)/7 = 19/(–7).

questions.q: Ritu works out (2/3) ÷ (3/10) as (3/2) × (3/10) = 9/20. Is she right? Find the correct quotient and name her slip.
questions.a: No. Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor (3/10), not of the dividend: 2/3 × 10/3 = 20/9. Ritu inverted the first fraction, so her 9/20 is wrong.
s: Names the slip: she inverted the dividend instead of the divisor

questions.q: Simplify (5/6) × (3/10 – 2/5) once directly and once using the distributive property, and show that the two results agree.
Write a rational number that is equal to 4/9, has a two-digit numerator greater than 40, and show with ad = bc that it is equal to 4/9.
questions.a: Multiply top and bottom by 11: 44/99. Check: 4 × 99 = 396 and 9 × 44 = 396, so 44/99 = 4/9.
s: Builds an equivalent fraction with numerator above 40 (such as 44/99)
Applies ad = bc with correct products
States the products are equal so the numbers are equal

questions.q: Take the rational numbers 3/4 and –5/6. (a) Find their sum and their difference (3/4 minus –5/6). (b) Find their product and the quotient of 3/4 divided by –5/6. (c) What do your four answers show about closure, and for which operation does closure fail if the second number were 0?
questions.a: (a) Sum = 9/12 – 10/12 = –1/12; difference = 9/12 + 10/12 = 19/12. (b) Product = –15/24 = –5/8; quotient = 3/4 × (–6/5) = –18/20 = –9/10. (c) All four answers are rational numbers, so rationals are closed under +, –, × and division; with a divisor of 0, division fails because the quotient is not defined.
s: Part (c): concludes closure and names division by zero as the exception

questions.q: Verify the distributive law for p = 9/5, q = 2/3, r = 5/6. (a) Find p(q + r). (b) Find pq + pr. (c) Name the law, and say why it helps to compute 9/5 × 2/3 + 9/5 × 5/6 in one step.
questions.a: (a) q + r = 4/6 + 5/6 = 3/2, so p(q + r) = 9/5 × 3/2 = 27/10. (b) pq = 6/5 and pr = 3/2, so pq + pr = 12/10 + 15/10 = 27/10. (c) Both equal 27/10: this is the distributive law p(q + r) = pq + pr; it lets us add the fractions first and multiply once.
s: Part (c): names the distributive law and its use

questions.q: For the annual day, Salma has 22 1/2 m of curtain cloth. Each curtain panel needs 1 7/8 m of cloth and a lace border of 2/5 m. She has 4 7/10 m of lace. (a) How many panels can she cut from the cloth? (b) Lace needed for all those panels? (c) By how much is the lace short or in excess? (d) The shop sells lace only in pieces of 1/2 m. Should she buy another piece for all the panels, or stitch borders on fewer panels? Decide, with figures.
questions.a: (a) 45/2 ÷ 15/8 = 12 panels. (b) 12 × 2/5 = 24/5 = 4 4/5 m. (c) 4 4/5 – 4 7/10 = 1/10 m, so she is short by 1/10 m. (d) A 1/2 m piece covers the shortage (lace becomes 5 1/5 m, 2/5 m more than needed), so buying one piece completes all 12 panels at the cost of a little waste; the alternative of bordering only 11 panels needs 22/5 m, which is within her 4 7/10 m but leaves one panel plain. Buying one piece is the better choice if all 12 panels must match; either is acceptable if justified with these figures.
s: Part (d): a justified decision using the shortage and the 1/2 m piece

questions.q: A school canteen sells peanuts in two packs: 3/4 kg for ₹54 and 5/6 kg for ₹65. The cook needs exactly 1 1/2 kg for sports-day snack packets. (a) Find the price per kg of each pack. (b) How much heavier is the bigger pack, as a rational number? (c) What is the cost of buying two packs of each kind, and how much weight would each purchase give? (d) Which purchase should the cook make? Justify with your answers.
questions.a: (a) 54 ÷ 3/4 = ₹72 per kg and 65 ÷ 5/6 = ₹78 per kg. (b) 5/6 – 3/4 = 1/12 kg. (c) Two small packs: ₹108 for 3/2 kg; two big packs: ₹130 for 5/3 kg. (d) Two small packs: they give exactly 1 1/2 kg, cost ₹22 less, and the price per kg is lower; the big packs bring 1/6 kg more than needed at a higher cost.
s: Part (c): ₹108 for 3/2 kg and ₹130 for 5/3 kg
Part (d): chooses two small packs with a reason from cost and exact quantity

questions.q: To mark 3/4 on the number line by the book's method, you should:
questions.a: divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts and move 3 parts right of 0
o: divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts and move 3 parts right of 0
divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 3 equal parts and move 4 parts right of 0
divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 7 equal parts and move 3 parts right of 0
divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts and move 4 parts right of 0

questions.q: The absolute value |–5/3| is equal to:
The distance between –9/2 and 3/2 on the number line is:
The rational number 9/4 lies between which two consecutive integers?
questions.a: 2 and 3

questions.q: Rani wants a rational number between 1/3 and 1/2 and uses the average of the two. Which number does she get?
On a straight road with the school gate marked 0 and east as positive, a library stands at –19/4 km and a bus stop at 9/4 km. How far is the library from the bus stop?
questions.a: 7 km

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: |x| is the distance of x from 0 on the number line.
Statement 2: The distance between two rational numbers a and b is |a – b|.
Statement 3: Between 1 and 3/2 there is no rational number because they are very close.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): There are infinitely many rational numbers between 1 and 2.
Reason (R): Between any two rational numbers lies their average, and this step can be repeated again and again.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: taking the average of 1 and 2, then of 1 and that result, and so on never runs out of new rational numbers.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. |–7/2|  2. The distance between 2 and –3  3. The average of 1/2 and 3/2  4. |0|
Column II: a. 7/2  b. 5  c. 1  d. 0
(a) Write 11/4 as a mixed number and say between which two integers it lies. (b) Describe how to mark it on the number line starting from the left integer.
questions.a: (a) 11/4 = 2 3/4, so it lies between 2 and 3. (b) Divide the interval from 2 to 3 into 4 equal parts and move 3 parts to the right of 2.
s: Part (b): divides the interval into 4 parts and moves 3 parts from 2

questions.q: (a) Find the distance between –5/6 and 7/6. (b) Show that interchanging the two numbers in |a – b| gives the same distance.
questions.a: (a) |–5/6 – 7/6| = |–2| = 2. (b) |7/6 – (–5/6)| = |2| = 2, the same, because a – b and b – a differ only in sign and the absolute value ignores sign.
s: Part (b): reverses the order and gets 2 again, giving the reason

questions.q: Why can the absolute value of a rational number never be negative? Give |–9/7| and |0| as examples.
questions.a: |x| is a distance from 0 and a distance cannot be negative, so |x| ≥ 0. For example |–9/7| = 9/7 and |0| = 0.
s: Gives the reason that |x| is a distance

questions.q: (a) Find the average of 3/4 and 7/8. (b) Show that the average lies between the two numbers.
(a) Find a rational number between –1/2 and 1/4 using the average. (b) Use that number and –1/2 to find a second rational number between –1/2 and 1/4.
s: Part (b): –5/16 as a second number in the interval

questions.q: Kabir says, '2.718 and 2.719 are so close together that no rational number lies between them.' Do you agree? Support your answer with a number.
questions.a: No. Rational numbers are dense: the average of two rational numbers lies between them. (2.718 + 2.719)/2 = 2.7185, which is rational and lies between them.
s: Cites the average of two rationals lying between them

questions.q: Show that no rational number x can satisfy |x| = –2/3.
questions.a: |x| is the distance of x from 0, and a distance is never negative, so |x| ≥ 0 for every rational x. But –2/3 is less than 0, so |x| can never equal –2/3.

questions.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/4 and 1/3 by taking averages, and write them in increasing order.
questions.a: The average of 1/4 and 1/3 is 7/24. The average of 1/4 and 7/24 is 13/48, and the average of 7/24 and 1/3 is 5/16. In order: 13/48 < 7/24 < 5/16.

questions.q: (a) Explain, step by step, how to mark –7/4 on the number line. (b) Between which two integers does it lie? (c) The point 5/4 is also marked. Write the distance between –7/4 and 5/4 using the absolute value and find it.
questions.a: (a) Divide each unit interval into 4 equal parts; start at 0 and move 7 parts to the left, since the number is negative. (b) –7/4 = –1 3/4, so it lies between –2 and –1. (c) |–7/4 – 5/4| = |–3| = 3.
s: Part (a): divides into 4 parts and moves 7 parts left
Part (c): |a – b| set up and value 3

questions.q: (a) Find the average of 1/2 and 3/4. (b) Use averages to find two more rational numbers between 1/2 and 3/4. (c) Explain why this process shows that you can never find the 'closest' rational number to 1/2.
questions.a: (a) (1/2 + 3/4)/2 = 5/8. (b) The average of 1/2 and 5/8 is 9/16 and the average of 5/8 and 3/4 is 11/16, so 1/2 < 9/16 < 5/8 < 11/16 < 3/4. (c) Whatever rational number is claimed to be next to 1/2, the average of it and 1/2 lies strictly between them, so another rational can always be found; there are infinitely many.
s: Part (c): the average gives a closer number each time, so none is closest

questions.q: On a straight canal road the school gate is 0 km, east is positive and distances are in km. The post office is at –7/4 and the bus stop at 5/4. A water kiosk is to be built so that the longer of the two walks (from the post office and from the bus stop) is as short as possible. (a) Find the distance between the post office and the bus stop. (b) Find the point halfway between them. (c) Find the walk from each to that halfway point. (d) If the kiosk were at the school gate instead, find the longer walk and decide where the kiosk should go.
questions.a: (a) |5/4 – (–7/4)| = 3 km. (b) The average (5/4 + (–7/4))/2 = –1/4. (c) |5/4 – (–1/4)| = 3/2 km and |–7/4 – (–1/4)| = 3/2 km. (d) From the gate: post office 7/4 km, bus stop 5/4 km, so the longer walk is 7/4 km, which is more than 3/2 km. The kiosk should be at the halfway point –1/4.
s: Part (d): longer walk 7/4 km from the gate and a decision for the halfway point

questions.q: A weather station at a hill station logs night temperatures in °C: Monday –7/2, Tuesday –9/4, Wednesday 1/2. Crops are normally covered when a night falls below –2 °C. (a) Which night is closest to 0 °C, and what is its absolute value? (b) Find the difference between the warmest and coldest night. (c) Find the average of the three temperatures. (d) A farmer says: 'The average is above –2, so I need not cover the crops on any night.' Is this a sound decision? Explain with your answers.
questions.a: (a) |–7/2| = 7/2, |–9/4| = 9/4, |1/2| = 1/2, so Wednesday is closest, with absolute value 1/2. (b) 1/2 – (–7/2) = 4 °C. (c) (–14/4 – 9/4 + 2/4)/3 = (–21/4)/3 = –7/4 °C. (d) The average –7/4 is above –2, but the average hides the individual nights: Monday (–7/2) and Tuesday (–9/4) are both below –2, so the crops should be covered on those nights. The farmer's reasoning is not sound.
s: Part (d): rejects the plan because two nights are below –2

questions.q: A square has each side 1 unit. By the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, its diagonal d has length:
questions.a: √2 units

questions.q: According to the book, who gave the first proof that √2 is irrational?
questions.a: Hippasus

questions.q: Proof by contradiction works by:
questions.a: assuming the opposite of the claim and reaching a logical impossibility
o: assuming the opposite and reaching an impossibility
checking the claim on many numbers until it always holds
dividing both sides by a common factor each time
drawing a careful figure and measuring all lengths

questions.q: The proof that π is irrational was given in 1761 by:
questions.a: Johann Lambert

questions.q: In the proof for √2 we reach 2q² = p². Neha says 'so p is even'. Her reason should be:
questions.a: p² is twice an integer, so p² is even and a number whose square is even is itself even
o: p² is twice an integer, so p² is even and p is even
q is even, so p must be even as well, since p/q is in lowest terms
p and q have no common factor, so p has to be even
√2 is irrational, so p must be even for that reason

questions.q: Following the construction of √2 (OA = 1 on the number line, a perpendicular at A, then an arc with centre O), Anita wants to mark √5. Which right triangle should she use?
questions.a: Legs 2 and 1

questions.q:
Read the statements about π.
Statement 1: Āryabhaṭa's value 3927/1250 = 3.1416 is the exact value of π.
Statement 2: Āryabhaṭa described 3927/1250 as an asanna, an approximation.
Statement 3: Lambert proved in 1761 that π is irrational.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): π is an irrational number.
Reason (R): Mādhava expressed π as an infinite series.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. π is irrational because Lambert proved it (1761); Mādhava's infinite series is how an exact formula for such a number can be written, not why it is irrational.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational we reach 2q² = p². (a) What can we say about p, and why? (b) Put p = 2k and show what this gives for q².
questions.a: (a) p² equals 2 times an integer, so p² is even, and a number whose square is even is itself even, so p is even. (b) 2q² = (2k)² = 4k², so q² = 2k².
s: Part (a): p is even because p² is even
Part (b): substitutes p = 2k to get q² = 2k²

questions.q: (a) What value of π did Āryabhaṭa give as a fraction, and what decimal is it? (b) Why did he call it only an asanna?
questions.a: (a) 3927/1250 = 3.1416. (b) An asanna is an approximation; he indicated that an exact fraction could likely not be found for π.
s: Part (b): says it is only an approximation and an exact fraction was not expected

questions.q: On the number line OA = 1 unit, a perpendicular AB = 1 unit is drawn at A and O is joined to B. (a) Find the length OB. (b) How is the point P that represents √2 obtained from it?
questions.a: (a) OB² = 1² + 1² = 2, so OB = √2. (b) With centre O and radius OB draw an arc cutting the number line at P; then OP = √2 and P represents √2.
s: Part (b): arc with centre O and radius OB meets the line at P

questions.q: Using the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem, show that the diagonal of a square of side 1 unit satisfies d² = 2. Why did this result trouble early mathematicians?
questions.a: d² = 1² + 1² = 2. They believed every length is a ratio of integers, but no fraction p/q has a square equal to 2 (√2 is irrational), so this length defied fractions.
s: Explains that the length cannot be written as a ratio of integers

questions.q: Why does the book say that a single fraction cannot give an exact formula for π, and what did Mādhava use instead?
questions.a: π is irrational, so no fraction (or finitely many fractions) can equal it. Mādhava used an infinite sum (series): π = 4 × (1 – 1/3 + 1/5 – 1/7 + …).
s: Links the impossibility of a fraction to π being irrational
Names the infinite series as Mādhava's method

questions.q: Isha says, 'From 2q² = p² we found p is even, so the proof that √2 is irrational is finished.' Is she right? Say what is still missing.
questions.a: No. She must also show q is even: with p = 2k we get q² = 2k², so q is even. Then p and q share the factor 2, which contradicts the assumption that p/q is in simplest form, and only this contradiction proves √2 irrational.
s: Says the proof is not finished
States the contradiction with p/q in lowest terms

questions.q: A craftsman cuts a rope of length 17/12 units for the diagonal of a unit square, saying it is exactly √2 because the value is so close. Show that 17/12 is not √2.
questions.a: If 17/12 were √2, its square would be 2. But (17/12)² = 289/144 and 2 = 288/144, so the square is 1/144 more than 2. Hence 17/12 is only a close approximation, not √2.

questions.q: Name the two legs of a right triangle, built on the number line as in the construction of √2, whose hypotenuse is √10, and another pair for √13. Verify each.
questions.a: For √10 use legs 3 and 1, since 3² + 1² = 9 + 1 = 10. For √13 use legs 3 and 2, since 9 + 4 = 13.
s: Checks the sums of squares are 10 and 13

questions.q: Write the proof that √2 is irrational in your own words, in the following steps. (a) State the assumption. (b) Show that p is even. (c) Show that q is even. (d) State the contradiction and the conclusion.
questions.a: (a) Assume √2 = p/q with p, q integers, q ≠ 0, in lowest terms (co-prime). (b) Squaring gives 2q² = p², so p² is even, hence p is even; write p = 2k. (c) Then 2q² = 4k², so q² = 2k², q² is even and q is even. (d) Both p and q are even, so they share the factor 2, contradicting that they are co-prime; so the assumption is false and √2 is irrational.

questions.q: A spiral is built on the number line: the first right triangle has both legs 1; every new triangle uses the previous hypotenuse as one leg and a new leg of 1. (a) Find the first four hypotenuses. (b) Find the hypotenuse of the 9th triangle. (c) Among the first ten hypotenuses, which are whole numbers, and why?
questions.a: (a) √2, √3, √4 = 2 and √5, since each squared hypotenuse is the previous one plus 1. (b) The nth hypotenuse is √(n + 1), so the 9th is √10. (c) The squares are 2, 3, …, 11; the perfect squares among them are 4 and 9, so the 3rd and 8th hypotenuses are the whole numbers 2 and 3.
s: Part (c): 2 and 3 because 4 and 9 are perfect squares

questions.q: A village temple committee lays a square fire-altar tile of side 1 unit, as in Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra. The mason proposes a diagonal rope of 17/12 units and his helper proposes 1.4 units. (a) Find d² for the diagonal by the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem. (b) Find the square of each proposed length. (c) By how much does each square differ from d²? (d) Which rope would you recommend, and can any fraction be the exact diagonal? Explain.
questions.a: (a) d² = 1² + 1² = 2. (b) (17/12)² = 289/144 and 1.4² = 1.96. (c) 289/144 – 2 = 1/144 (about 0.007 too big) and 2 – 1.96 = 0.04 (too small). (d) The 17/12 rope is closer (error 1/144 against 0.04), so recommend it; but neither is exact, because the exact diagonal is √2, which is irrational and equals no fraction p/q.
s: Part (d): recommends 17/12 and says √2 is irrational

questions.q: A history club prepares a note on π. Āryabhaṭa (499 CE) gave 3927/1250, Lambert proved π irrational in 1761 and Mādhava gave an infinite series in the 14th century. A craftsman needs the rim length of a circular altar of diameter 10 m, and the club compares Āryabhaṭa's value with the school value 3.14. (a) How many years after Āryabhaṭa's value did Lambert's proof come? (b) Find the circumference 10π with each value. (c) By how much do the two lengths differ? (d) Which value should he use, and can either give the exact circumference? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 1761 – 499 = 1262 years. (b) With 3927/1250: 10 × 3.1416 = 31.416 m; with 3.14: 31.4 m. (c) 31.416 – 31.4 = 0.016 m, i.e. 1.6 cm. (d) Use Āryabhaṭa's 3.1416 if the 1.6 cm matters, while 3.14 is enough for rough work; neither is exact, since π is irrational and no fraction or finite decimal equals it.
s: Part (d): a justified choice and the remark that π has no exact fraction

questions.q: Without dividing, which fraction (in lowest terms) has a terminating decimal expansion?
The decimal expansion of 21/80 terminates. How many digits come after the decimal point?
Irrational numbers have decimal expansions that:
questions.a: never end and never repeat
o: never end but repeat a block
repeat a block of at most 6 digits

questions.q: When 1 is divided by 7 the decimal must repeat because:
questions.a: only six non-zero remainders are possible, so one must appear again and the steps loop
o: only six non-zero remainders occur, so one must return
7 is an odd number, so the digits can never stop coming
the remainder 7 keeps coming back at every step
the quotient digits are always 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7 in turn

questions.q: Rohan sees the fraction 21/35 and says, 'The denominator 35 has the prime factor 7, so the decimal repeats.' What is the correct conclusion?
questions.a: It terminates, since 21/35 = 3/5 = 0.6
o: It repeats, since 7 is a factor of 35
It terminates, since 35 = 5 × 7 has a factor 5

questions.q: In dividing 1 by 13, Pooja writes the remainders 1, 10, 9, 12, 3, 4 and then 1 again. What can she conclude?
questions.a: A block of 6 digits repeats forever
o: A block of 6 digits repeats forever
A block of 12 digits repeats forever

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: 11/40 has a terminating decimal expansion.
Statement 2: 5/12 has a terminating decimal because 12 is an even number.
Statement 3: A decimal that does not terminate must be irrational.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The decimal expansion of 5/11 is a repeating decimal.
Reason (R): Every rational number has a terminating decimal expansion.
questions.a: The assertion is true (5/11 = 0.454545…) but the reason is false: a rational number's decimal either terminates or repeats, and many (such as 5/11 and 1/7) repeat.
o: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Match each number in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. 3/8  2. 5/11  3. √2  4. 0.999…
Column II: a. Terminating decimal  b. Repeating decimal  c. Non-terminating, non-repeating decimal  d. Equal to 1
(a) Show that 13/250 has a terminating decimal by factorising the denominator and rewriting the fraction with a power of 10 below. (b) Write the decimal.
questions.a: (a) 250 = 2 × 5³, so multiplying top and bottom by 4 gives 52/1000, a power of 10 below. (b) 52/1000 = 0.052, with 3 decimal places.
s: Part (a): 250 = 2 × 5³ and denominator 1000 after multiplying by 4

questions.q: (a) Divide 5 by 11 to obtain the first six decimal digits. (b) Name the repeating block and say how many digits it has.
questions.a: (a) 5/11 = 0.454545… (b) The block is 45, which has 2 digits.

questions.q: (a) Write 9/16 as a fraction with denominator a power of 10. (b) State the decimal and the number of decimal places, and relate that number to the factorisation of 16.
questions.a: (a) 16 = 2⁴, so multiply top and bottom by 5⁴ = 625: 5625/10000. (b) 9/16 = 0.5625, with 4 decimal places, the power of 2 in 16.
s: Part (b): 0.5625, 4 places equals the power of 2

questions.q: When we divide by 7, (a) why can a remainder never be 0 while dividing 1 by 7? (b) What happens once a remainder appears a second time?
questions.a: (a) A remainder of 0 would mean the division ends, but 7 does not divide 1, 10, 100, … so the remainders are among 1 to 6. (b) The steps that follow repeat exactly, so the digits loop and the decimal repeats.
s: Part (a): only remainders 1 to 6 occur, 0 would need 7 to divide a power of 10 times 1
Part (b): the whole division loops, giving a repeating decimal

questions.q: Look at 0.2020020002… in which the number of zeros between the 2s grows by one each time. (a) Does it terminate or repeat? (b) Is it rational or irrational? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) It does not terminate and it does not repeat any block, because the gaps keep growing. (b) It is irrational: only rational numbers have terminating or repeating decimals.

questions.q: Dev says, '21/35 has the factor 7 in its denominator, so its decimal repeats.' Is he right? Find the decimal.
questions.a: No. The test is applied to the fraction in lowest terms: 21/35 = 3/5, and 5 is only a factor 5, so the decimal terminates: 3/5 = 0.6.

questions.q: Show that 5/12 cannot be a terminating decimal. (Hint: a terminating decimal can be written as k/10ⁿ.)
questions.a: If 5/12 = k/10ⁿ then 5 × 10ⁿ = 12k, so 3 would divide 5 × 10ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 5ⁿ⁺¹. But that number has only the prime factors 2 and 5, so 3 cannot divide it. Hence 5/12 is not terminating (its denominator 12 = 2² × 3 has the factor 3).
s: Notes 5 × 10ⁿ has only the prime factors 2 and 5
Concludes the factor 3 in 12 makes this impossible

questions.q: Write a fraction in lowest terms with denominator less than 50 whose decimal terminates after exactly 3 places, and another with denominator less than 20 whose decimal repeats. Justify both using prime factors.
questions.a: Example: 3/8 = 0.375: 8 = 2³, so there are 3 places. Example: 5/6 (or 1/7): 6 = 2 × 3 has the factor 3, so the decimal 0.8333… repeats.
s: A terminating fraction with denominator giving 3 places (such as 2³ or 5³ or 2³ × 5)
A repeating fraction whose denominator has a prime factor other than 2 and 5

questions.q: Without long division, classify 7/16, 5/18, 29/200 and 17/45 as terminating or repeating. (a) Give the prime factorisation of each denominator and your classification. (b) For the terminating ones, state how many decimal places each will have. (c) Write the terminating ones as decimals.
questions.a: (a) 16 = 2⁴ and 200 = 2³ × 5²: terminating; 18 = 2 × 3² and 45 = 3² × 5 contain 3: repeating. (b) 7/16 has 4 places; 29/200 has 3 places (the larger power of 2 and 5). (c) 7/16 = 0.4375 and 29/200 = 0.145.
s: Part (a): factorises all four denominators and classifies

questions.q: Divide 1 by 13. (a) List the remainders until one repeats. (b) Write the repeating block of 1/13 and its length. (c) Find the 100th digit after the decimal point.
questions.a: (a) The remainders are 1, 10, 9, 12, 3, 4 and then 1 again. (b) 1/13 = 0.076923076923…, so the block is 076923 with 6 digits. (c) 100 = 16 × 6 + 4, so the 100th digit is the 4th digit of the block, which is 9.

questions.q: A tuck shop prices items per gram: dry dates ₹7/16, roasted gram ₹5/12 and peanut chikki ₹11/40 per gram. The bill printer can show only exact decimals with at most 2 decimal places. (a) Which of the three per-gram prices have terminating decimals, and with how many places? (b) Find the price of 100 g of each as a rational number and say which ones print exactly. (c) The roasted-gram price repeats; what weights in grams make its price a whole number of rupees? (d) The owner must choose between rounding the roasted-gram bill to the nearest paisa or selling that item only in lots of 12 g. Which would you recommend and why?
questions.a: (a) 7/16 = 0.4375 (16 = 2⁴, 4 places) and 11/40 = 0.275 (40 = 2³ × 5, 3 places) terminate; 5/12 = 0.41666… repeats. (b) 100 × 7/16 = ₹43.75 and 100 × 11/40 = ₹27.50 print exactly; 100 × 5/12 = 125/3 = ₹41.666… does not. (c) A multiple of 12 g, such as 12 g costs ₹5. (d) Selling in lots of 12 g keeps every bill exact (12 g costs ₹5, 24 g ₹10) with no rounding loss, so it is the more accurate plan; rounding is simpler for customers but each bill is a fraction of a paisa off.
s: Part (a): which terminate and the number of places

questions.q: A maths club sorts cards without dividing: 17/40, 13/22 and 9/125. (a) Say which cards have terminating decimals and give the number of decimal places for each of those. (b) The card 13/22 begins 0.5909090… Name the repeating block, and find the 20th digit after the decimal point. (c) The notice board allows only 2 decimal places. Round each card to 2 places and find the error for each (distance from the true value). (d) The club says, 'Terminating decimals lose less when rounded than repeating ones.' Is this supported by your answers?
questions.a: (a) 17/40 = 0.425 (40 = 2³ × 5) with 3 places and 9/125 = 0.072 (125 = 5³) with 3 places terminate; 13/22 (22 = 2 × 11) repeats. (b) The block is 90 (the 5 comes first and does not repeat); the 20th digit is 9. (c) 0.425 ≈ 0.43 has error 0.005; 0.072 ≈ 0.07 has error 0.002; 13/22 ≈ 0.59 has error about 0.0009. (d) No: the repeating decimal has the smallest rounding error. Whether a decimal terminates tells us about its form, not how much is lost on rounding.
s: Part (d): rejects the claim with the evidence

questions.q: The terminating decimal 0.45, written as p/q in lowest terms, is:
Let x = 0.6666… (the 6 repeats). Multiplying by 10 and subtracting gives 9x = 6, so x equals:
To convert x = 0.1666… (a single 1, then 6 repeating) to p/q, the book multiplies x by which two powers of 10 and then subtracts?
The product 142857 × 4 equals:
Arjun lets x = 0.999…, multiplies by 10 to get 9.999… and subtracts to get 9x = 9. What does he conclude?
questions.a: x = 1, so 0.999… is exactly equal to 1
o: x = 1, so 0.999… is exactly equal to 1
x is a little less than 1
x = 9, so 0.999… is a whole number nine

questions.q: Kavya writes x = 0.1555… (only the 5 repeats) as p/q by multiplying by 10 and by 100 and subtracting. Her answer should be:

Read the statements.
Statement 1: 0.999… = 1.
Statement 2: A terminating decimal such as 2.47 also has the form 2.46999… with repeating 9s.
Statement 3: 142857 × 2 = 285714 uses the same six digits as 142857, moved along.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 0.2323… = 23/99.
Reason (R): With a two-digit repeating block we multiply by 100 and subtract, which gives 99x = 23.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: 100x – x = 23.2323… – 0.2323… = 23, so 99x = 23 and x = 23/99.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Match each decimal in Column I with its fraction in Column II.
Column I: 1. 0.4545…  2. 0.1666…  3. 0.35  4. 0.999…
Column II: a. 5/11  b. 1/6  c. 7/20  d. 1
(a) Convert x = 0.2727… to p/q in lowest terms. (b) Check your answer by dividing the numerator by the denominator.
questions.a: (a) Two digits repeat, so 100x – x = 27, 99x = 27 and x = 27/99 = 3/11. (b) 3 ÷ 11 = 0.2727…, which matches.

questions.q: Write as fractions in lowest terms: (a) 0.064 (b) 4.375.
Convert x = 0.2333… (the 3 repeats) to p/q. (a) Which two multiples of x do you subtract? (b) What fraction do you get in lowest terms?
questions.a: (a) Multiply by 10 to move the non-repeating digit (10x = 2.333…) and by 100 to move one repeating cycle (100x = 23.333…); subtract: 100x – 10x = 21. (b) 90x = 21, so x = 21/90 = 7/30.

questions.q: (a) Find 142857 × 5 and say what you notice about the digits. (b) Find 142857 × 7 and say how it matches the fact that 1/7 × 7 = 1.
(a) Write 2.47 in the alternative form that has repeating 9s. (b) Use the same idea to write 0.5 with repeating 9s.
Tara says, '0.999… must be a little smaller than 1, because the 9s never reach the 1.' Do you agree? Use algebra.
questions.a: No. Let x = 0.999…; then 10x = 9.999…, and subtracting gives 9x = 9, so x = 1. Hence 0.999… is exactly 1; the book notes that a terminating decimal has an alternative with repeating 9s.
s: Sets x = 0.999… and subtracts to get 9x = 9

questions.q: Rahul says 0.0909… equals 9/100 because 'the digits are 0, 9, 0, 9'. Show that this is impossible and find its true value.
questions.a: 9/100 = 0.09 terminates, while 0.0909… never ends, so they cannot be equal. Let x = 0.0909…; the block 09 has two digits, so 100x – x = 9, 99x = 9, x = 9/99 = 1/11.

questions.q: Write a pure repeating decimal that equals 1/33 and prove it with the subtraction method.
questions.a: 0.030303… Let x = 0.0303…; the block 03 has two digits, so 100x – x = 3, 99x = 3, x = 3/99 = 1/33.
s: Multiplies by 100 and subtracts to get 99x = 3

questions.q: Convert x = 0.7363636… (the block 36 repeats after the single digit 7) to p/q. (a) State the numbers of non-repeating and repeating digits. (b) Say which multiples of x you take. (c) Subtract and solve for x. (d) Write the lowest form and check it by long division for the first few digits.
questions.a: (a) One non-repeating digit (7) and two repeating digits (36). (b) 10x = 7.3636… and 1000x = 736.3636…. (c) 1000x – 10x = 736 – 7, so 990x = 729 and x = 729/990. (d) Dividing both by 9 gives 81/110; 81 ÷ 110 = 0.7363636…, which matches.
s: Part (a): one non-repeating and two repeating digits

questions.q: Write each as p/q in lowest terms: (a) 15.4 (b) 1.375 (c) 0.2323… (d) 2.1666… (the 6 repeats).

At a school maths fair, a stall shows that 1/7 = 0.142857142857… and that multiplying 142857 by 1 to 6 only shifts its digits around. A visitor asks whether the same trick works for 13. The stall owner knows 1/13 = 0.076923076923…, 3/13 = 0.230769230769… and 2/13 = 0.153846153846…. (a) Find 142857 × 4 and say which fraction's decimal block it matches. (b) Without dividing, write the repeating block of 5/7. (c) Show that the block of 3/13 is the block of 1/13 shifted. (d) Should the stall display 'every fraction n/13 for n = 1 to 12 uses the digits 076923'? Decide, giving evidence.
questions.a: (a) 142857 × 4 = 571428, the block of 4/7 = 0.571428…. (b) 142857 × 5 = 714285, so 5/7 = 0.714285…. (c) 076923 shifted left by 3 places gives 230769, the block of 3/13. (d) No. The block of 2/13 is 153846, which is not a shift of 076923, so the 12 fractions fall into two separate cycles (n = 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12 use 076923, while n = 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11 use 153846). The claim is false for 13, unlike the neat case of 7.

questions.q: A cycling track in a Pune school ground has one lap of exactly 0.3636… km (the block 36 repeats). The sports teacher marks laps using 0.36 km. The school plans a 25-lap race. (a) Write the lap length as p/q in lowest terms. (b) By how much does the true lap exceed 0.36 km, as a fraction of a km? (c) Over 25 laps, how far short (in metres, to the nearest metre) will a race of 25 laps of 0.36 km be? (d) Which lap length should the teacher use to place the finishing line, and why?
questions.a: (a) 100x – x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11 km. (b) 4/11 – 9/25 = (100 – 99)/275 = 1/275 km. (c) 25 × 1/275 = 1/11 km ≈ 91 m (true race 100/11 ≈ 9.09 km against 9 km). (d) Use 4/11 km (the exact value): 0.36 km would put the finish about 91 m short; a rounded decimal loses a little on every lap and the loss builds up.
s: Part (d): recommends 4/11 km with the accumulated error as the reason
